speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate in debate on what I think is a very important issue facing our country today. The motion talks about the problems we are having with trade in the forest industry and in the agriculture industry.
The problem in the forest industry is a bilateral one with the United States because our trade is taking place with the United States and our problem is protectionism in that country. Regarding agriculture, the problem is slightly different because the United States Farm Bill subsidizes exports of American grain and it subsidizes American farmers. The

March 18, 1986
Supply
problem with the Farm Bill is that it will disrupt world agricultural markets. Those are the two problems we face.
Today's motion speaks directly to a very important issue our country is debating today while the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is in the United States, and that is the whole issue of free trade with the United States. I want it to be very clear that 1 oppose a comprehensive free trade arrangement between the United States and Canada because it is more than just economics. A free trade arrangement will create a level playing field where economic integration will mean that the same rules that apply in Alabama will apply in Saskatchewan, and that will eventually lead to cultural, social and political integration.
Free trade is a question of independence for this country. It is a question of our sovereignty and our very nationhood. If we have a problem now with so much of our economy owned by the United States and 77 per cent of our trade with the United States, just think of the problems we would have if we had a comprehensive free trade agreement with the United States. We would always be going cap in hand to Washington.
When the Prime Minister was running for the leadership of his Party, he said in Thunder Bay that he opposed a free trade arrangement with the United States. He also said that the Liberals tried it with Laurier and lost an election, and that a free trade arrangement with the United States was like a mouse going to bed with an elephant, in that the mouse might feel very secure until the elephant rolled over. I agreed with the Prime Minister of the country when he said that. I think he was right then but he is wrong now. It is really a question of the mouse and the elephant.

And that is why, Mr. Speaker, this motion is extremely important. It is very important in the forestry industry, a sector vital to the creation of jobs here in Canada. It is also very important for Canadian farmers across the country. The problem for us in Canada is the protectionist policies of the United States. With protectionism in the U.S., we have unemployment here in Canada, a lot of it in the forestry industry and among our Canadian farmers. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said three years ago, it's like a struggle between a mouse and an elephant, because the population of the United States is now over 200 million, while Canada's population is only 25 million.
To me, free trade is not just a matter of economics. It is also a matter that involves Canada's independence, Canada's sovereignty, and forestry is a vital industry. I hope that today and tomorrow, our Prime Minister will have a serious discussion about this matter with President Reagan in the United States. It is important for Canada. It is important for Quebec and British Columbia and Ontario. It is important because 300,000 people work directly in this industry. There are also 700,000 people working indirectly in the forestry sector here in Canada. There are many lumberjacks and a lot of other people
that depend on this industry. It is Canada's most important export industry, and last year, its economic value to Canada was $25 billion. Mr. Speaker, the Wilson Budget contains a cut in Government spending on the forestry sector.

The other issue is the U.S. Farm Bill. I cannot help but use the rest of my remarks asking colleagues on all sides of the House to rally with us in trying to point out to the Americans the danger of that Bill to Canadian farmers. Let us look at the headlines which have appeared in newspapers over the last few days and weeks. An article in the Manitoba Co-operator was entitled "U.S. Farm Bill will hurt". One in The Globe and Mail was entitled "U.S. Farm Bill could hurt Canada". In a story in The Toronto Star, the following was indicated: "Moves toward U.S. export subsidy may prove worrisome for Canada". Finally, an article appeared in The Western Producer which was entitled "Situation may lead to subsidy battle". Newspaper after newspaper are starting to tell Canadians about the danger of the American Farm Bill to our country.
I should like to spend a few minutes talking about that Bill. It became law in the United States toward the end of 1985. It is to become effective in June, 1986, or in about two or three months. It is a big threat. Why is it a big threat? What will it do? It will allow the American Secretary of Agriculture the power to reduce the export price of American farm products to other countries around the world. Also it will allow the American Secretary of Agriculture to increase subsidies to American farmers. Why are the Americans doing that? It is because of their sagging exports, because of their increased inventories of grain, particularly wheat, and because of massive subsidies by the European Common Market in what is amounting in reality to an all out trade war between the Treasury of Europe and the Treasury of the United States of America.
What will be the cost of this American Farm Bill? Mr. Speaker, even though you are not from a western Canadian riding, I am sure you will realize our problems. Over the next three years a conservative estimate, if I could use that word, of the cost to the United States will be $52 billion. That is what the Americans will be spending to subsidize the export of American farm products and to subsidize the income of the American farmer.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-VIABILITY OF FORESTRY AND AGRICULTURAL INDUSTRIES
speechtext: So much for free trade.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-VIABILITY OF FORESTRY AND AGRICULTURAL INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
I hear the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin). Free trade for whom? We are living in a fool's paradise if we think seriously that the Americans want free trade with Canadians. I think the Prime Minister is starting to realize that. Now he talks more about enhanced trade than he talks about free trade. In any event, the Americans will spend $52 billion in the next three years, and perhaps more. The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool is estimating that it will be over $60 billion in the next three years. What will the Americans do? First, they will subsidize the export of American food products to various countries around the world.
March 18, 1986

Second, they will subsidize the price of a bushel of wheat and the price of other farm products to American farmers.
Who will suffer? It will be the farmers of Canada, Australia, Argentina and New Zealand; they will be the victims of the American farm Bill. Our Treasury cannot compete with the Treasury of the United States or with the Treasury of the European Common Market. It is important for the Prime Minister to take a message to Ronald Reagan saying that the farm Bill is wrong and that the problems of the international grain economy or of the farm economy cannot be solved by building huge protective walls around the United States and having a trade war with the European Common Market.
How will the Bill work? The system in the United States is similar to ours in terms of advancing money to farmers before they sell their grain. In Canada it is called cash advances. In the United States it is called a loan rate. The only difference is that the American Government takes possession of the grain, whereas we just make an advance on what a farmer will receive when his grain is sold. The loan rate for wheat in the United States this year will probably be set, according to agricultural economists, at $2.40 per bushel. The loan rate automatically becomes the floor price of wheat, not just in the United States but on a global basis, because the Americans have 25 per cent of the world share of wheat production and we have only 5 per cent. If the price of wheat falls to $2.40 per bushel, how many Canadian farmers will survive? We do not have a program to subsidize our farmers like the one of the Americans. The United States now has a support level for wheat of $4.38 per bushel. If the world price is $2.40 per bushel on one hand and the support price is some $4.38 on the other hand, there is a difference of $1.98 which is made up by the Treasury of the United States. In other words, a subsidy of about $2 per bushel will come from the Reagan administration to the grain farmers of the United States. The victims of this will be the farmers of Canada because the Canadian Wheat Board cannot compete under any circumstances with $2.40 per bushel wheat anywhere in the world. Many of our importing customers will be waiting until June until the American farm Bill becomes law. Asian countries, African countries and even the Soviet Union will be looking to the United States where they can buy grain for $2.40 and $2.50 a bushel instead of paying a higher price here in Canada. We are in very serious difficulty, Mr. Speaker.
I checked the Chicago futures market for the price of wheat. In the month of March wheat is quoted at $3.40 a bushel. Do you know what it is for the month of July, Mr. Speaker? It is down to $2.50 a bushel, a drop of 90 cents a bushel. I ask you, how will farmers survive with the price of grain at $2.50, $2.40 or $2.60 a bushel, which is what the indication now is from the U.S. farm Bill and the Chicago futures market?
The Canadian Federal Grain Marketing Bureau spokesperson, Gary Moore, said recently that we can anticipate a drop in the price of wheat of between 20 per cent and 30 per cent in the calendar year 1986-87. You can anticipate a drop in the
Supply
income of wheat farmers of $1 billion in the next crop year because of the American farm Bill. This farm Bill applies not only to wheat but to many other commodities. They are all listed in those summaries that we have seen accompanying that legislation. It works the same way. For example, there will be a subsidy of about $1 a bushel for soy beans.
What is the purpose of the farm Bill, Mr. Speaker? It is to try to drive down the price of grain in the world because the Americans feel that the European subsidy is too high. The Americans are trying to drive down the price of grain to break the backs of the European countries, a bit of a daredevil's war of who is going to say "uncle" first, the Europeans or the Americans. It is a battle of two Treasuries. It is a bidding war between the Europeans and the Americans.
The farmer in Kamsack, the farmer in Lethbridge, Yorkton or Kindersly is caught in the middle of this bidding war between the United States and the Europeans. The question is, what can we do about it? There are a couple of things. The Prime Minister is in Washington today. He must look at Ronald Reagan eyeball to eyeball, square in the eye, and tell him that his farm Bill will bankrupt thousands upon thousands of farmers across Canada and that he must not proceed with the U.S. Farm Bill. Second, the Prime Minister must initiate discussions with the President of the United States toward the beginning of an international wheat agreement, an effective and comprehensive international grains agreement where the price of wheat will have some reflection on the cost of production for farmers around the world.
We used to have such an agreement. It broke down in 1969 when the United States of America started to sell wheat below the agreed upon floor price. Because the Americans are the biggest producers of wheat in the world, they broke the agreement and destroyed the whole guaranteed pricing system for farmers around the globe.
What we have now is the law of the jungle. What we have now is the law of Rambo. If you are big and strong, if you are muscular and have all the devices of a massive Treasury behind you, you can subsidize your farmers and screw farmers in other countries. That is what we are seeing with the United States Farm Bill. This Parliament must speak as one, loudly, clearly, emphatically and aggressively. We must say that that is not good enough.
We have to support agriculture in Canada because if the farmer is better off, then we are all better off. If the farmer is better off, there are jobs in towns and cities for the young people of Canada. If the farmer makes $2 or $3, he will spend $7 or $8. That is why we have to defend agriculture.
This is a very important debate today. This Parliament must say to our Prime Minister, as this country said to Laurier many years ago, "We don't want a free trade agreement between Canada and the United States. We know that a free trade agreement between the two countries will affect more than just economics, it will affect our very political sovereignty, our very independence as a nation". Our vision of trade in the world must go beyond the shores of North America. Our vision must include China, the developing world, Japan and

March 18, 1986
Supply
the Pacific Rim. Our vision must include as well increasing production for Canadians. If we have free trade with the United States of America we will see a loss of jobs and a loss of some of the social programs that we know and we will see a loss of the very autonomy and the very nationhood of our country. We will see it affecting the farmers, the Canadian Wheat Board, the poultry industry and the dairy industry.
The time has come for Canadians from coast to coast to rally behind the flag of this nation, this great country of Canada, to stand up and to fight for ourselves with the patriotism that other countries such as the U.S., France and Britain have shown for years and years and years.

Mr. Speaker, it is a matter that involves Canada's sovereignty and Canada's independence. It is time to act.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-VIABILITY OF FORESTRY AND AGRICULTURAL INDUSTRIES
speechtext: Are there any questions or comments? If not, we will continue debate. The Hon. Member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pern broke (Mr. Hopkins).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-VIABILITY OF FORESTRY AND AGRICULTURAL INDUSTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is quite true that the debate taking place in this House today is of the utmost importance to Canada and to our future. Ever since the pioneer days of Canada, agriculture and forestry have been two major staples of the Canadian economy. Fewer and fewer people are participating in agriculture now, but the industry has certainly grown in great bounds of production right across the country.
We have had other staple crops, such as, for instance, fish and fur. But to drive the point home as to why today's debate on forestry today is of extreme importance let me say that 11 per cent or more of the Canadian labour market work in the forest or forest related industries. There is no way we can go into trade negotiations thinking that we are going to come away with a pat on the back and everything will be all right. We have to do our homework ahead of time. Hard bargaining is simply good business. The U.S. understands that very well. The Americans have been good bargainers over the years and that spells their success.
I suppose bargaining can best be illustrated by using the case of the cattle drover. He goes out to buy cattle and he goes to those farmers from whom he got the best deal last year. If we as a nation end up being a poor bargainer, then we will be had and more people will take us for a ride.
The Americans will not respect Canadians any more if we are the soft-touch in any free trade agreements. They understand hard business bargaining and will respect us more if we are tough than if we take everyting with a smile.
In relation to the jurisdictional structure of the forest industry in Canada it is important to point out that in my view one of the greatest weaknesses of the Canadian Constitution is the fact that the national Government in Canada does not have direct control over the natural resources of the country. They
are, rather, under provincial jurisdiction. In the United States natural resources are under the jurisdiction of the national Government in Washington. That allows more direct action. Can you imagine having to deal with every state in the United States if those resources were under the jurisdiction of the various states?
On the very basis of our Constitution we have great difficulty dealing with forest-based industries and the management of our forests. The management of our forests in crucial to this entire argument. We must have good quality timber in the years ahead to compete favourably.
This morning during a question and comment period the Hon. Member for Levis (Mr. Fontaine) condemned the Government for not having reforestation programs and for selling lumber without putting the proceeds back into the Canadian forest industry. He was saying that natural resources in Canada are under federal jurisdiction, which they are not. The forest resources in Canada are under provincial jurisdiction. I wonder what the Quebec Government would have done if the federal Government had gone into the Province of Quebec and started doing the work which legally belongs to the Department of Natural Resources of that province. We would have a real constitutional wrangle.
Let us get it straight. The provinces have always been in charge of managing the forests of the country. We all realize that some of them have done a very poor job. Based on its forest resources, British Columbia should be in far better shape than it is today. The forests in the Province of Ontario were the milch cow of a Conservative Government for over 40 years until the recent change. The money made from the forests were not used for the renewal of natural resources in the Province of Ontario. I suspect that you will Find the same situation in many other provinces of Canada. In order to compete favourably, we must have our own house in good order.
The free trade issue is one of the most critical issues facing the Canadian economy today. There is no sense in denying it. There is a great deal of concern within the farming community across the country. There is a great deal of concern among sawmill operators, lumber dealers, and all forest-related industries. There should be concern in the labour community of Canada as well as in the business community. As I just said, over 11 per cent of the labour population of Canada works in forest-related industries.
The Minister of International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) and the Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) must sell their ideas to the forest-based industries of the country. They must talk to the farmers of the country who are very ill to ease and need real assurances. Free trade has implications for all regions and all economic sectors of Canada. How well we conduct the negotiations and how well we achieve the objectives of those negotiations will have an enormous impact on all of us for years to come. A closer analysis of a free trade agreement shows that some Canadians would gain and some would lose. It shows that some of the losers would be the textile and the agricultural industries.
March 18, 1986

A previous speaker in this debate talked about the problem between the European Economic Community and the United States. It certainly is a battle in dollars between the United States subsidization of their agricultural industry and the subsidization by the European community of their farmers. It remains to be seen who will win that dollar battle. We suspect that it will be our neighbour to the south. The European countries are already suffering from the high cost of subsidizing their agricultural community. They would desperately love to get out of that situation and lower those subsidies, but they do not dare to do so because the Party which does it will lose the next election. Farms in Europe are still small and farmers have a lot of clout. With so many political Parties, every vote is important.
Paula Stern, the United States' chief watchdog on trade, is not sure of the benefits of free trade with Canada. Free trade is clearly not supported by a majority of Canadians. Liberals have always supported freer trade, but not free trade, that is, a reduction of both tariff and non-tariff barriers, but not at the expense of our sovereigty, cultural identity, or ability to make our own economic decisions. If our economy is such that we are the captives of an international agreement, we will certainly be giving up a large part of our sovereignty and the right to make major economic decisions.
Any discussions must recognize the unique needs of the Canadian economy and Canadian society. The danger of being railroaded into a hasty decision now might later prove to be damaging to Canadian interests. Can we trust the Government's negotiating abilities? That question is on the mind of many Canadians. Time and again we have seen the Government cave in to the slightest pressure. The meeting in Quebec City between the President of the United States and the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) one year ago was seen as a meeting of total agreement followed by a good bash. Canadians reacted to that with suspicion of this very close liaison. They were worried about what was really being given away. The facts are there, Mr. Speaker.
The other thing which started the spirited national debate between the United States and Canada in recent months was the issue of the Polar Sea. When the Polar Sea was going through the Northwest Passage there was no comment from the Government of Canada. That led Canadians to believe that the Prime Minister was indeed too cosy with the President of the United States. It again comes down to good business bargaining. You cannot have good business bargaining if you are willing to give anything away just to be a friend.
To date the Government has not provided us with an assessment of the costs by sector and region. Hundreds of questions remain to be answered. Some of the provincial Premiers have caused the Government to accept provinces as part of the negotiations because the provinces have too much at stake. They have too much at stake for the very reason I mentioned a while ago. The forest resources of the country are under the jurisdiction of individual provinces. That is a big source of income for provincial Governments and naturally
Supply
they are going to be very concerned about what type of deal this Government strikes with the U.S. on the forest industry.
Farmers throughout the country are strongly opposed to free trade. The cultural industry is in a state of confusion and concern over free trade. Thousands of jobs could be lost if negotiations are not handled carefully and with resolve. If we look at the possible effects on agriculture, we have to look at the subsidization of some sections of the industry such as the dairy industry. We must make certain that agriculture is not on the negotiating table. How do you prevent this? I suspect the Government will put it on the table. If I heard the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) correctly, he recently said that if there was not a good agreement on agriculture with regard to free trade, there would be no agreement. Those are very brave words and I hope he means them. Farmers throughout this country will be watching the Minister very carefully to make sure he backs up those words.
Federick Stokelo, Director of International Business Relations for the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, said:
I hate to say this, but U.S. business with Canada is treated as business in California.
He means that Canada is indeed treated like the 51st state. That statement comes from an American, not a Canadian.
The potential loss of supply management and agricultural marketing boards would prove disastrous. Twenty-five per cent of all Canadian farmers are in serious financial difficulties and the industry needs to be protected. Not only that, it needs to be supported. In the recent Budget we saw $700 million set aside for loans to the agricultural community. At the same time there are from 50,000 to 60,000 farmers who are facing financial risk if not bankruptcy. In farming today $100,000 is not very much when it comes to equipping the farm and putting it on a solid footing. Even if you lowered the amount of a loan to $100,000 on average, that money set aside will only go to service about 7,000 farmers. There will still be more than
50,000	with the same problems.
This is indeed a big challenge and it must be looked at seriously. Agriculture in Canada can no longer be looked upon as a way of life where people live on the farm because it is their home. It is not only their home, it is a place of business. Agriculture today is serious business. You can drive along a country road and see a large farming operation and not realize that there is more money invested in that farm than perhaps in a factory that you had just passed going through the local town. I use that example in order to emphasize the fact that we have to protect the agricultural industry as well as the forest industry in these negotiations. Until the Government gives those two industries some realistic responses to these problems, the people concerned cannot have any real faith in these negotiations. People who have been working for years to build up a farm or a sawmill operation are really going to be behind the eight ball if they see that these negotiations could mean the failure of their operation.

March 18, 1986
Supply
The Prime Minister said that sleeping with an elephant is terrific until he twitches or rolls over. Perhaps that phrase has been used enough. He also added that this is why the question of free trade was decided in the election of 1911, when it was defeated. It affects Canadian sovereignty, and we will have none of it, not during leadership campaigns or at any other time. That is what he said. Canadians are going to be watching closely to make sure he lives up to what he says.
I will not go over the time allowed me but I wish I could take a minute to talk about the U.S. Farm Bill and how some of its provisions will affect Canada. However, the bottom line is that those provisions are certainly going to affect Canada's trade. They are certainly going to affect our capacity to maintain a strong base in the farm industry. Hopefully we will be able to upgrade our forests and get some good research going in Canada, but the bargaining in that sector will have to be tough.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade, 1 would like to make a few additional comments on the motion introduced by my colleague from Skeena (Mr. Fulton).
With respect to the American Bill on agriculture, the Farm Bill, the Government is seriously concerned about the unfavourable impact this legislative measure might have on the Canadian agricultural community.
Just for the record I would point out that President Reagan signed the Farm Bill last December 23 when it became law after a protracted debate in Congress.
Basically the Bill deals with the levels of price support and income for various products, and some of its provisions are
11638

March 18, 1986
Supply
trade related. As in the case of a number of domestic American legislative measures, the Farm Bill has had a serious impact on Canada's agricultural community. Our Government conveyed to the American authorities our deep concern about these provisions which will have negative repercussions on Canadian exports and farm income.
Generally speaking, we expressed concern about the over-all approach of a legislative measure which is likely to isolate American producers from the international marketplace.
The Bill guarantees support prices above market levels for American producers while exports would be subsidized in certain cases. We are concerned about American measures aimed at stimulating production artificially and overemphasizing direct export assistance to such an extent that it would depress world prices even more and perhaps be detrimental to Canadian exports.
We have expressed our deep concern about the extensive use of export subsidies to increase American exports of agricultural products. We are especially concerned about the Export Premium Program and the Targeted Export Assistance Program, both of which we consider direct export subsidies. Under the first, $2 billion in surplus public stocks must be placed at the disposal of American exporters at no cost as premiums to promote business sales and the development of export markets. The second program requires that $325 million in cash or in surplus public stocks be used for targeted export activities.
We have indicated to the American authorities that we believe these programs to be inconsistent with the support given by the United States to multilateral initiatives aimed at bringing about agricultural subsidies under control, and especially at preventing export subsidies for unprocessed agricultural products. In addition, to the extent that these programs would apply to processed agricultural products, they would be inconsistent with the commitments of the United States under GATT.
We have expressed our concerns about various other forms of export assistance which could have a detrimental effect on world markets, such as the continuation of short term export credit guarantees; the creation of a renewable credit fund for farm exports; the extension of intermediate credit for exports; and the development of pilot program to barter farm products for strategic resources.
We have also spoken about the dairy herd reduction program, which could cause an upheaval on the North American processing beef markets.
We have strongly protested against a number of provisions in the Bill which could eventually restrict access to the American market. In the case of sugar, for instance, we have expressed deep concern about the provisions which would have removed the Canadian allocation in the American quotas for
sugar imports. We have told the American authorities that we consider these provisions inconsistent with the commitments of the United States under GATT. We have raised the issue of a possible application of the regulations on chemical residues to limit Canadian cattle and cattle product exports. We showed concern about prescribing discriminatory assessments on some cattle imports. We made it known that such measures did not conform with United States commitments under the GATT. Finally, we raised objections to a provision which was definitely aimed at restricting the potato trade by requiring spot checks and ongoing inspections of Canadian potato shipments entering through Northeastern ports.
The U.S. Government shares some of our concerns respecting the trade provisions in the Farm Bill and has attempted to have them removed. In some cases, efforts made by the Administration and our representations have been successful.
For instance, we succeeded in obtaining the removal of a provision that would have resulted in the loss of Canada's quota of sugar exports. Furthermore, we are convinced that the provisions concerning chemical residues will not hamper Canadian exports of cattle and cattle products.
The Administration has indicated it still is concerned about some of the trade provisions. Upon signing the Farm Bill, on December 3, President Reagan expressed some reservations. He indicated: "This legislation commands export subsidies that could well turn against the United States''. The President added that he intended "to try, in conjuction with Congress, to correct those problems, especially in the area of trade".
In response to those efforts, the Congress has now passed the Food Security Improvement Act of 1986, amending some provisions of the 1985 Farm Bill. The President should be signing the new Act soon.
On the trade level, amendments to some provisions in the Farm Bill are now under way. For instance, the value of Government surplus commodities required for the grants in kind program is reduced from $2 billion to $1 or $1.5 billion. The value of Government surplus products or monies required yearly for the targeted export assistance program is to be reduced from $325 million to $110 million during fiscal years 1986 to 1988. Although those reductions are a step in the right direction, subsidizing levels still are high and we will maintain our pressures for a more satisfactory solution.
This Government continues to make representations to the U.S. Administration suggesting that they look with Congress for a solution that would alloy our concerns.
The concerns raised by the Farm Bill once more show that bilateral and multilateral trade talks are important if we are to study those issues and, more importantly, prevent other protectionist bills from coming into force.
As it has been indicated by American authorities, a major part of the trade provisions in the Farm Bill are based on the inability of the Administration to reduce what is perceived as
March 18, 1986

unfair trade practices on the part of the United States major trade partners. In that respect, one of the goals supported both by the United States and Canada, which is sprucing up before entering into bilateral and multilateral trade talks, is improving on the rules governing farm trade and strenghtening the access of farm products to markets.
Mr. Speaker, let us hope that this Government can rely on the support of the Opposition parties when it enters into those negotiations.
Turning to lumber, my colleague the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) referred to a criticism levelled in the House of Representatives against Canada's Natural Resources Subsidy Bill, a criticism that was referred to the Chairman, Mr. Gibbons. In view of the particular concerns expressed by Members of the Opposition regarding the proposed legislation, I think it would be useful to advise them of the Government's views concerning it. Since the criticism is short and to the point, I will read it in full.
The dual pricing provision of the Bill would amend the countervailing duty law of the U.S. to expand unilaterally the definition of subsidy to include situations in which a natural resource is made available to foreign producers of downstream products at a price lower than the world market price or export price. The dual pricing provision has the following main shortcomings. First, proposals to define dual resource pricing policies as countervailable subsidies represent a fundamental departure from longstanding U.S. practice under legislation reflecting agreed international disciplines. These recognize that domestic programs which are generally available to more than a specific enterprise or group of enterprises do not constitute a countervailable subsidy. A radical departure from this approach, such as envisaged by H.R.-2451, would establish a precedent which could be extended to a wide range of policies and programs which differ from jurisdiction to jurisdiction, for example, tax policy, education and other social programs, irrigation and conservation. Generally available benefits, such as controlled oil prices in the 1970s, have been defended by the U.S. as not constituting a countervailable subsidy. Canada and the U.S. share a common interest in ensuring that the general availability concept is not eroded.
Second, to require that resources be sold in resource rich foreign jurisdictions at international prices established by export cartels, or less competitive producers, would be anticompetitive and perverse in its consequences. For these reasons the dual pricing provision is unacceptable to Canada.
The removal rights provision would amend the countervailing duty law to permit a finding of subsidization where no subsidy exists. This provision is not intended to deal with dual pricing policies. Rather, a determination of subsidy would be based on a finding of whether a Government's price for the right to exploit a resource is lower than the fair market value of that right, arbitrarily defined. Fair market value would be
Supply
determined by simply using the price paid for removal rights in the country with the largest number of arm's length sales of such rights outside the country under scrutiny. In the case of forest products, Canadian prices for trees would be compared to U.S. prices for trees. If the Canadian prices for a comparable right in a comparable region are not as high as U.S. prices, then the difference would be deemed a countervailable subsidy.
The key question is why the U.S. price should be the bench-mark. First, this proposal presumes to deny other jurisdictions their legitimate right to pursue policies which differ from those pursued by the United States. To suggest that such policies should be deemed to confer a countervailable subsidy simply by virtue of the fact that they differ from U.S. policies is neither reasonable nor acceptable.
Second, the price of a natural resource in situ in one country tells us nothing about what the price for the same type of natural resource should be elsewhere. In the case of softwood lumber, the U.S. Commerce Department's decision, after a thorough investigation, demonstrates why the proposal in H.R. 2451 would be unfair. The decision states that it would be "arbitrary and capricious" to compare Canadian stumpage prices with U.S. stumpage prices in view of, inter alia, "the wide differences between species composition; size, quality and density of timber; terrain and accessibility of the standing timber throughout the United States and Canada; and the additional payments which are required in many provinces in Canada but not generally in the United States". In other words, comparing the price paid for Canadian trees-which tend to be smaller, harder to log and less accessible-with the price of U.S. trees totally ignores the realities of the marketplace. Yet the removal rights section would require this comparison to be made.
For all the reasons outlined in this critique Canada concludes that the removal rights proposal is wrong in principle and unwarranted.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us today expresses our concern with respect to two resource areas which are important to many parts of Canada. In fact, every province of Canada has some investment in these two resource areas.
My constituency of Prince Albert is basically an agricultural constituency. However, in the constituency there is a pulp mill. A large proportion of the population of the City of Prince Albert have jobs related to that pulp mill. So we are talking about two resource areas which are directly affected by action, in this case legislative action, by the great friendly giant to the south. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), has covered the effects of the possible legislation

March 18, 1986
Supply
coming up in Congress with respect to forests. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), expanded on the issue. He pointed out the effects of the U.S. farm Bill, which has just been passed, and which is just starting to affect the markets of the world. He also pointed out how it affects Canadian farmers. I, too, wish to spend a few moments on the effects of the 1985 U.S. farm Bill on Canadian farmers.
During 1985, U.S. farm commodities became uncompetitive in world markets. The declining farm income contributed a great deal to the already severe financial crisis faced by farms in the United States. This was a financial crisis which was matched, and which was perhaps even worse, than ours. As a result of sagging exports, since they were not competitive, large volumes of American grains were allowed to accumulate over a fairly long period of time. Those stocks, along with declining farm incomes, became an issue in the United States which forced the passage of the U.S. farm Bill. I suppose it should be pointed out that the farm Bill was not a favourite piece of legislation of the present administration. In fact, it was reluctantly signed by the President. The Bill authorizes the Secretary of Agriculture to reduce market prices to a more competitive level. At the same time it allows him to protect farmers' incomes by increasing the prices paid to farmers. In other words, even as the price of commodities is decreased across the world, the price paid to the farmer will continue to increase.
It would appear that Canadians are not the only program junkies. We see that the American farm Bill includes many very lucrative programs in some cases and programs aimed at reducing the amount of product on the market in other cases. It contains programs like the parity price programs, the soil bank, the acreage reserve, the conservation reserve, the payment in kind program, target prices and loan prices. These are all programs which are a part of the American farm Bill.
As 1 mentioned previously, the motion before the House is in two parts. One part deals with forestry and one with agriculture. There is one difference between these two industries as far as the problem is concerned, though both industries have a problem with trade and export. In the case of the forest industry, the problem is due to our penetration of the American market. We have increased our portion of the United States softwoods market to approximately 45 per cent. That is greatly resented by the lumber producing states and they have taken action against it. We feel a certain amount of compassion for that action. I hope that we would do the same thing if it happened to us.
The challenge facing agriculture is a little different. In agriculture, we are not penetrating the U.S. market to any extent except perhaps in the red meats area. Here the U.S. legislation is affecting the international markets. In the agriculture sector, Canada is a price taker rather than a price setter. In a great many sectors which concern us particularly, the United States is a price setter. Consequently, it is important that we deal with the United States and its relationship to the world market.
There are three points which should be made regarding the U.S. farm Bill. These are the three points which affect us. When looking through the technical Bill, we find that a number of products are affected, but a great deal of concern has been expressed about the use of land in the Bill and the attempts to reduce production by paying surprising subsidies under certain conditions.
The points in the U.S. farm Bill which affect Canada are, first, the way the Bill affects the price of grain overseas. The second point is that the aim of the farm Bill is to assist in the increase of U.S. exports to the markets of the world. This is done first by affecting the price. Lowering the price would directly affect the income of Canadian farmers. Second, because the Americans are increasing their exports to the markets of the world, they are moving into markets which we have traditionally accepted as being our markets. Therefore, that reduces the amount of commodities we may sell into those same markets.
Americans seem to be overwhelmed by the drop in their market share. They used to have about 35 per cent to 40 per cent of the world market. Beginning in about 1974, that share of the world market rose considerably and averaged something over 50 per cent for a short period of time. That share of the grain markets of the world has now dropped back to approximately 35 per cent to 40 per cent.
The third point with which we have to deal when looking at the farm Bill is that it reduces the cost of feeds in the United States and consequently reduces the cost of feeds in Canada. This will affect all meat producers. There is likely to be an increase in the production of red meats in particular both in the United States and in Canada as well as in the production of poultry and other so-called white meats. There is likely to be an increase in the production of livestock in the United States and that will reduce the amount of exports that we will be able to make of those products into the United States. It reduces our penetration of the U.S. market for those products and consequently we cannot expect to take advantage of the reduced cost for the price of feeds to increase income from the production of livestock.
How does the U.S. farm Bill affect the price of grains? I think that question has been covered to some extent previously so I will deal with it very quickly as it is a point which needs to be made because it is the basis of our concern. The U.S. loan price, which is technically a floor price for world grain prices, has been reduced by 27 per cent for wheat. It is down to approximately $2.40 per bushel. The price of Canadian red spring wheat can be expected to fall by an equal amount. These prices will probably fall by 30 per cent. This means that the price of No. 1 grade would fall to approximately $145 per tonne, a drop of $45 per tonne. The price of the lower grades will probably fall to $3 per bushel. The price of Ontario wheats may go as low as $115 per tonne. This price is far below the cost of production.
March 18, 1986

There is a further aberration in the export market caused by the American policy of increasing exports from the United States. As the previous speaker mentioned, last May the Government of the United States made available $2 billion to increase exports from the United States. Of course these subsidies were aimed at certain countries and certain markets, particularly the North African market. That United States grain was equal in quality to our No. 2 and No. 3 western spring wheat, and it was exported to Egypt and Algeria at approximately $100 per tonne. That is a level with which no farmer in the world can compete. 1 know it was aimed at the European market, but it had the effect of reducing the sale price of wheat around the world.
I could provide the same type of technical information on barley, coarse grains and corn. Corn will be reduced by 25 per cent on the loan rate. The effect on barley in Canada will be approximately the same. We can expect approximately $2 per bushel or $90 per tonne for western barley after the U.S. farm Bill comes into effect. Of course there will be slightly higher barley rates in Ontario. Oil seeds will not be affected because the soya bean reduction in the U.S. farm Bill was only 5 per cent. Soya bean and canola reductions will probably be 10 per cent or thereabouts. However, the producers of every one of those grains will experience a reduction in income.
The Bill will also affect the livestock industry. Chase Econometrics has indicated that possily the livestock industry will remain the same or be a little better. However, the statistics of the Government of Canada and those of the Government of the United States do not indicate that. Because of the lower price of feed and because of higher production in the United States and in Canada, the result will likely be lower prices in the livestock industry. There will possibly be less of a chance to sell livestock, which will also force down the price. The projected income of cattlemen because of the U.S. Farm Bill will either remain the same or be forced downward. The situation will be the same for hog production for exactly the same reasons. There may be an increase in the number of hogs, but the result will probably be a lowering of the price.
In summary, grain prices will be pushed down. Livestock prices may not be pushed down as much, but they will be affected negatively. The United States is putting some $52 billion into farm subsidization over a three-year to five-year period, and Canada cannot begin to compete with the Treasury of the United States.
What can be done? I should like to take a few minutes to put forward some possibilities. We must first recognize the problem immediately. We must ensure that the United States knows the effect of its actions on us. Also we must negotiate for more favourable action on the part of the United States. Then we must take action in Canada to ensure that we have adequate programs in place to allow for the survival of the family farm and the agricultural industry. They will be attacked by the effects of the U.S. farm Bill which was put in
Supply
place to protect its farms. We must do something to protect our farms as well.

Mr. Speaker, when the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) was speaking, I could not help but think that the U.S. Farm Bill is important and vital to Canada and that it might be wise to get all three Parties together to come up with a unanimously supported joint resolution in the House expressing our concern about that Bill. I see that the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) has just left the Chamber. Perhaps he could get together with spokespersons in the other two Parties to see if we can come up with a joint resolution. The wording of our resolution might not be exactly what the Minister wants. It has been worded in the parliamentary context of condemning the Government; that is the way we do things around this place. 1 see the Hon. Member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) across the way. Perhaps he is in agreement with what 1 am saying and could take the initiative before the afternoon is out to try to come up with something of that sort.
It is important to impress upon Americans that we as Canadians feel very strongly about the U.S. farm Bill, which will subsidize their grain and other agricultural exports by $52 billion over the next three years. This will hurt Canadian farmers, as will a war between the Treasury of Europe and the Treasury of the United States. When exported grain from the United States is subsidized massively in places such as the Soviet Union, Asia and North Africa, and when the American farmer at home is subsidized as well, the price of grain falls. As I mentioned earlier this afternoon, the price of grain on the Chicago futures market has already fallen to around $2.30 per bushel. It will fall by another 90 cents between the month of March and the month of July.
If I am not mistaken, shortly we will hear an announcement in the House by the Minister of State for Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) of a drop in the initial payment to farmers. Farmers are in serious difficulty. They call upon the House to exert some leadership, to put aside some of our petty partisan differences, and to speak with a united voice to the United States of America and to President Reagan. They call upon us to say that when the farm Bill comes into effect in June it will hurt Canadian farmers. It will mean that farmers from one part of the country to another will go broke, and it will mean a loss of jobs.
I wanted to make those comments. I appeal to the Government across the way. Perhaps there is some way to come up with a joint resolution of the House. I see the Minister for International Trade is now present in the Chamber. For his benefit I repeat briefly that it would be very nice if we could come up with a joint resolution of the House to express to the American Congress and the American Senate how we feel about the American farm Bill. I know there is a consensus on the matter. Perhaps we in all three Parties, over the next couple of days, can come up with some way of expressing it unanimously to the American administration; it might be very useful. Perhaps the Hon. Member for Prince Albert could comment on it.

-because that is the direction we should be taking. I am pleased that the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Mel-ville (Mr. Nystrom) will perhaps lead his Party in a slightly different direction and give us all the support we need.
I am happy to have this opportunity to respond to the motion because I know the U.S. farm Bill is on the minds of many Canadian farmers. I am also pleased to have this opportunity to set the record straight on the inaccurate assumptions upon which the motion is based.
The last time the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) and Mr. John Block, former Secretary of Agriculture in the United States, met in Canada they announced the formation of a joint horticultural committee composed of representatives from Canada and United States industries to correct and resolve existing trade differences between the two countries. The process has already started.
We have to recognize that we are dealing with a new phenomenon today. The Opposition seems to be looking backwards, looking at things that have passed instead of looking to the future, a glorious future that we may have in world society. We do, however, have some problems which world society has not had to face before, the European Economic Community and also a very strong United States economy. We have to make sure that we are not hurt in the process. That is what this exercise is all about.
There is no question that the U.S. Farm Bill carries with it serious consequences, not only for Canada but for producers in other countries as well. I think it would be fair to say the provisions are aimed at the Europen Economic Community, yet countries such as Canada are bound to experience some fall-out. We have to make sure that that fall-out will do us as little damage as possible.
The United States is a huge trading nation. Thus it has the ability to influence world commodity prices in a way that Canada, and most other trading nations, cannot. It would be a mistake to assume anything different. We have neither the level of trade nor the treasury to compete in the subsidy war.
We in Canada, however, can benefit from being a good neighbour to the United States. Perhaps members of the Opposition are not aware that before you can have a good neighbour you must first know how to be one. Respect and trust cannot survive and last for any length of time on a one-way street.
The U.S. Farm Bill allows the Secretary of Agriculture to reduce U.S. loan rates per bushel of wheat and feed grains to a maximum of 20 per cent below the basic rate in 1986-87. The formula for setting loan rates in the following years is being finalized. In essence though the Secretary can reduce the loan rates a further 5 per cent each year. This has placed severe downward pressure on world grain markets. Further pressure is also resulting from the two export assistance programs.
In the longer term, the Farm Bill may tend to reduce U.S. wheat production toward the end of the 1980s. In the shorter terms, "payment in kind" from Government stock as part of deficiency payments and as export subsidies will maintain
March 18, 1986

downward pressure on gain prices. U.S. grain stocks are expected to remain high for the balance of the 1980s unless export demand strengthens marketing.
The United States Government tried to control production somewhat, Mr. Speaker, by bringing in what they called the payment in kind or the PIK Program. The Government of the United States did not achieve the success it hoped it would under that program because farmers were paid to take a percentage of land out of production. The land they took out of production was the poorest producing part. They increased fertilizer and chemical use for weed control and produced just as much grain. That is why the PIK Program was not as successful as the United States Government had hoped it would be.
The Minister of Agriculture spoke with the former Secretary of Agriculture at considerable length about this Bill when he visited Canada recently. The U.S. administration is well aware of our concerns, and the lines of communication remain open. In fact, even as I speak, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is in the United States meeting with the President, and I am confident this issue will be raised.
I might just bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, an excerpt from Parliamentary Alert, a publication which many Members get. I would like to read it for the benefit of the House. Under the heading "Prime Minister in Washington", it reads:
Ottawa interest will shift from Parliament Hill to Washington this week as Prime Minister Mulroney travels to the U.S. capital for talks with President Reagan. Trade and acid rain are the main subjects of interest on the agenda.
The Prime Minister's Washington visit has been stretched to cover four days.
This is significant because when foreign diplomats journey to other countries visits are only for one day, but this one is for four days. The article continues:
He arrives from Montreal Monday evening, to be greeted by Secretary of State George Schultz.
Tuesday morning he meets with President Reagan for an hour in the Oval Office. Following lunch at the State Department he travels to Capitol Hill to meet members of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. The day will end with dinner at the White House. Wednesday morning he has breakfast with Vice-President George Bush, and then returns to Capital Hill to meet members of the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Back to the White House he joins President Reagan for a working lunch in the family quarters. He will then visit Arlington Cemetery and end the day with dinner at the residence of the Canadian ambassador A. E. Gotlieb. A farewell ceremony will take place at the Reflecting Pool Thursday morning.
That makes sense to me, Mr. Speaker, as I am sure it does to a lot of Canadians. That is the way to deal on tough issues and that is the way to create understanding and goodwill. If there was ever a time in Canadian history when we needed good understanding with our friends south of the 49th parallel, it is now. There is no question that the subsidies contained in the Farm Bill are not helpful to Canadian grain growers, but the Government is doing all it reasonably can in response.
In that regard, I would like to commend my colleague, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), for the initiative he has shown on behalf of Canada's grain farmers. He has initiated a series of meetings with four
Supply
other major grain and oil seed exporters: Australia, Argentina, the United States, and the EEC. Together, through negotiation, perhaps we can sort out the concerns about trade and subsidies that we are discussing today.
One fact that will always speak well for Canada in international markets is the quality of our grain. We remain committed to maintaining the highest standards. In doing so, we are protecting an international reputation which will continue to serve the industry well. It is still unclear how, or if, the Farm Bill's dairy herd termination program will affect Canada. We may know more by April as the administrative details are worked out.
At this time, however, we have obtained assurances from the United States Department of Agriculture that the program will be managed in such a way as to minimize disruptive effects on the North American beef markets. For example, the American Commodity Credit Corporation is required to buy 400 million pounds of meat under the program, half of it for domestic food programs. This should reduce the chances of a sudden massive glut on world markets. We are continuing to monitor this program closely and, as I said, are keeping the lines of communication open between our two countries. This is very important.
My colleague, the Member for Blainville-Deux-Montagnes (Mrs. Landry), mentioned the problem we have with regard to beef producers. Beef producers in Canada form one component of our agricultural industry which is competing well with its counterpart south of the border. This is why enhanced trade is so important to beef producers in Canada. One thing we can do is to produce beef well.
We cannot control world commodity prices. Canada certainly cannot win a subsidy war with the United States, or the European Economic Community for that matter. However, through domestic programs we can assist producers who are faced with low commodity prices. Of course, we must be careful to strike a balance between the need for assistance and the need to keep the borders open to our key export markets.
Our most recent domestic program to respond to low commodity prices is the $700 million Commodity Based Loan Program. This program recognizes the fact that a farmer's ability to meet his loan payments is tied to the rise and fall in commodity prices. This program was one of several important provisions for farmers contained in the last Budget.
One of the things which many people seem to forget is the benefits which will accrue to farmers as a result of the latest Budget introduced by the Government. It is our stabilization programs which primarily serve producers during periods of low commodity prices. Due to the Government's initiatives, our agricultural stabilization network is stronger and more effective than it has ever has been. For instance, we amended the Western Grain Stabilization Program to trigger a record initial payment last spring. We anticipate another significant pay-out this spring, as the Minister responsible for the Wheat Board mentioned today in response to a question during Question Period.

Supply
Tripartite stabilization for the red meat sector is now a reality and a success story in the country. That is again due to the leadership shown by the Government and the faith it puts in consultation. Stabilization plans for red meat now represent between two-thirds and three-quarters of a hog, fed beef, and lamb production in the country. I am confident that more provinces will sign for more commodities in the future. For the first time in Canada, thousands of red meat producers have the opportunity to participate in an equitable national plan which cushions them from downward price swings. Other types of producers also benefit from payments under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. In fact, since we have been in government more than S483 million worth of payments have been made to Canadian producers under this Act.
Now and in the future Canada's farmers will reap the benefits of the actions the Government has taken to strengthen the structure of the farm industry through better, more effective stabilization programs. This brings me to the second part of the motion. Far from failing to take measures for farmers, the Government has in fact introduced far more agricultural initiatives of far greater significance than Canada's farmers have seen in many years. I am going to take a minute to list a few in order to refresh the memories of the Members opposite.
We introduced a $500,000 capital gains tax exemption on the sale of farm property. The NDP fought that. It did not want to give farmers that break. We introduced farm fuel tax rebates. In the February 26 Budget we extended the rebate program to 1988, and we are getting rid of some of the red tape. Farm Credit Corporation interest rates have dropped to their lowest level since 1979. We extended the small business bond program. We earmarked $80 million to reduce interest rates on about 5,400 Farm Credit Corporation loans. We are establishing farm debt review panels and are supplementing them with effective legislation aimed at strengthening the farmers' negotiating position. We provided drought assistance to prairie farmers amounting the $200 million in 1985, and we are working with the provinces to improve crop insurance coverage for producers who have endured consecutive years of drought. This program is moving ahead for the benefit of farmers. Crop insurance will certainly be a great benefit to farmers in the future.
We placed a high priority on agriculture at the First Ministers' Conference, and there have been productive follow-up discussions with provincial Governments on ways in which we can work together to serve farmers more effectively, such as the crop insurance plan I just mentioned. If that plan is to work, it must be carried out in conjunction with the provinces.
We acted to halt the flood of subsidized beef from the European Economic Community in 1985 reducing imports to less than half of the 1984 level under the previous administration. We have taken further action on behalf of Canada's beef industry for 1986. We doubled the size of loans for advance payments on grains. We introduced a long-term dairy policy representing a federal commitment to Canada's dairy farmers of close to $300 million annually.
In short, Mr. Speaker, the Government has introduced nearly 200 agricultural initiatives worth more than $4 billion-since it has taken office. The Budget of February 26 singles out the farm sector, perhaps more than any other, for further assistance. That is action, that is delivering, that is commitment. We are going to keep on taking action, keep on delivering and keep on placing a high priority on agriculture because we are determined to see Canada's farmers through to better and more prosperous times. I thank the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Minister of Agriculture for their assistance in helping us to put those programs inplace for the Canadian farmer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not a case of being anti-American. It is a case of being pro-Canadian. It is making a stand on our traditions, culture, experience and our ways of doing things. I remember someone who used to grace this House of Commons for many years starting in 1935. He was premier of our province for 17 years and then came back here in the early 1960s. He was accused of being anti-American. Tommy Douglas said: "I like Americans. They are nice people. They are good neighbours. They are good friends". He said: "I like my relatives, too. I like my friends. But I don't want them taking over my house and my having to live in the garage."
Canada, by itself, cannot do very much to stop any decision that the U.S. administration and Congress decide to make. We can, however, do more to remind our good friends and good neighbours to the south about our traditions and practices. They have said over the past number of years, in fact I think since my hon. friend from Red Deer came here, that the Canadian Wheat Board was somehow subsidizing to grain producers and therefore it was unfair. Bless his dear departed soul, although there was not much good we could say about
Supply
him it was R. B. Bennett who started the Canadian Wheat Board. It was not put into practise until about 1939 or 1940, and that was just because of the war, but he started it. It was a principle of orderly marketing. Yet Americans are saying they want the issue of hog marketing agencies in our provinces on the table.
You can ask hog producers in Saskatchewan and la belle province about the system they have devised, totally under provincial jurisdiction, to help protect the marketing capacity and incomes of hog producers. That has always been questioned by our friends south of the border. Our dairy, poultry and egg producers have always been challenged by U.S. Governments on those organizations which they collectively and voluntarily set up for themselves through their provincial and national Governments to try to protect themselves. It was to try and make their industry and the results of their labour a lot more viable.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is in Washington right now. That is fine. We enjoy it. They are going to have him over for a steak dinner, and perhaps in the swimming pool tonight. Who knows? That is nice. It is good that leaders of countries get together in a friendly, informal manner. It is not a case of being anti-American; it is asking our national Government and this Parliament to remind the Americans and to ask them to show some respect, regard and understanding for our rights, traditions, history and methods of doing things, many of which are historically different from theirs, just as they would like to receive from us, our respect for them, for their nation and their people for exactly the same things, their rights, traditions and history. It is a two-way street. Just because they are bigger than us-if they really are, and 1 believe they are-a nation that gives first place to showing respect for the independence and the sovereignties of other nations, they have to be persuaded, by whatever means we can find, not to do the things they have done in the past and what they are proposing to do now. My colleague the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), pointed out very well earlier today just what is in store for us in the forest industry alone.
I believe that an overwhelming majority of the American public do not know or do not understand what is happening, and that is what we have been asking in this resolution. There are groups who think that you can negotiate a free trade arrangement between a small nation and a big nation. If one considers Canadian history and the history of other countries in the British Commonwealth, in the southern Pacific, in Asia and in Africa, one finds that in the days when we were colonies we all got what was called the empire preferential tariff treatment. Even after 1930, after the statute of Westminster, there were still countries in the British Commonwealth that were colonies that got that preferential treatment. Right up until the Second World War even Canada got that preferential tariff treatment. We had most of our eggs, at that time, in Great Britain, our trading eggs.

March 18, 1986
Supply
Up to and during the Second World War we provided Britain with most, if not all, but certainly the largest part, of their butter, cheese, bacon, ham and beef. When the war was over, so much for having all of our eggs in one basket. Most of that market we lost within a very few years. What are we doing? We are in the process of putting our eggs in one basket again. It seems to me-and I say this to the Minister in all sincerity-that we could do more on a commodity by commodity basis, bilateral agreements in terms of quantities, minimum maximum prices, and let the market play around from there for a given period of time by agreement with a number of countries in a host of commodities. We should not rely on the economy of some large power. Even the Hungarians have got out of being totally dependent on trade with the Soviet Union. There have been some very complimentary articles in the North American press about their moving out into trading with other countries of the world. We are in a similar position economically, not ideologically.
I get a little tired in the middle of February of paying $2, $3 for a head of cauliflower and a buck and a half or $2 for a pound of tomatoes at the supermarket. 1 went to Mexico for a couple of weeks about a year ago now. There is a country which desperately needs some hard currency. In this country you ought to see the tomatoes they grow and the cauliflowers. Those people may be poor but they are mostly not hungry and they produce.
Why do we not make a deal, perhaps a straight barter arrangement, with Mexico on things such as purebred cattle, dairy herds, apples or Canadian wine in exchange for fruits and vegetables, especially in the five or six-month period of the year when we cannot grow anything here except snowballs? You could make a deal with Mexico, the Caribbean countries and Central America.
I must even fault the co-operative movement, of which I am an ardent member and supporter. I found out that the Federated Co-Ops from Thunder Bay to the Pacific Ocean do not buy their own fresh fruit and vegetables; they buy them through Scott National. Who is Scott National? It is a subsidiary of the multinational corporation that has all those farms in Arizona, California and Florida. We could not even sell the fresh vegetables grown in the Qu'Appelle Valley north of Regina to the local supermarkets in Regina. We had farmers in the Qu'Appelle Valley up to here in potatoes, turnips, cabbages and corn who could not sell them 20 miles away. Why? Because somebody else controls what is coming into this country, at what price and when. How long are we going to hold still for that? I hope all my colleagues find that somewhat embarrassing in terms of what we can and should be doing ourselves, among ourselves and with many other nations in the world.
Caribbean and Southeast Asian countries grow things that we can use and there are things that we have that they could use. We do not have to be in a situation where 80 per cent of our exports are to the United States.

Seventy-seven per cent, all right. Sixty-five per cent of our imports from Americans come here. The trouble is that the other 35 per cent that they do not export to Canada is handled by U.S. corporations in Canada, and the heads of the U.S. companies in Canada get their orders at the end of a telex. So much for your economic sovereignty and independence.
I believe very sincerely that the United States administration and Congress and the American people would fully respect and recognize Canada speaking up and standing up for itself in that full, frank, firm and straightforward manner, whether it is our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) meeting with the United States President or MPs and Senators meeting with U.S. Congressmen and Senators, or businessmen here meeting with businessmen there. They will understand and respect that because they expect the same kind of understanding and respect themselves. They get that from us. They have no respect for this hands and knees syndrome in which we crawl down and plead and beg them to honour and respect us as a sovereign and independent nation. Again, it is what Tommy Douglas called many years ago, "this supine acquiescence". If the American administration and Congress tell us to jump, we ask how high. I find that demeaning, i don't blame the Americans for that, I blame us. The time is overdue that we told not only the United States but other nations that we are willing to negotiate, to bargain and make deals because we respect how they operate, but we expect the same from them.
I recall the years of the international wheat agreements that marked a milestone in international trade and understanding among many countries. Who killed those agreements?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-VIABILITY OF FORESTRY AND AGRICULTURAL INDUSTRIES
speechtext: The Americans.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 82-VIABILITY OF FORESTRY AND AGRICULTURAL INDUSTRIES
speechtext: Who killed the international grains arrangement? As soon as it infringed on what the Americans believed were their rights, they killed an agreement that was a milestone for the grain trade in Canada. We must continue to fight for our rights as a nation on behalf of Canadians and our national independence.
