subtopic: HEALTH-EXPOSURE OF WORKERS TO CIGARETTE SMOKE. (B) SMOKE-FREE OFFICES-ECONOMICS SAVINGS
HEALTH-EXPOSURE OF WORKERS TO CIGARETTE SMOKE. (B) SMOKE-FREE OFFICES-ECONOMICS SAVINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question that I want to pursue at this time is extremely important. It concerns the health of Canadians, particularly those who work in areas under federal jurisdiction.
The question I raised with the Minister of National health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) specifically dealt with two studies which documented the extent of lung cancer deaths among people who are not smokers, but involuntary smokers. These are studies which show how very expensive smoking is in the federal workplace and how much money would be saved by introducing controls.
It is not only very interesting, but shameful that the studies were obtained by the Non-Smokers Rights Association under the Access to Information Act because they had not been published. The Minister said that at least one would be published. One of the studies dates back to January, 1984 and certainly could have been published. The sad fact of the matter is that the harm caused to involuntary smokers and the deaths among involuntary smokers as a result of smoking is much greater than imagined.
Let us consider that the so-called acceptable risk of developing lung cancer from involuntary smoking is 6 to 7.5 per
100,000	smokers every year. While I will not go into the details, that is a reasonable calculation. The amount of contaminant required to produce a rate above that acceptable level is reached when one person out of 60 smokes one cigarette a day. Consequently, it does not take an excessive amount of tobacco smoking to reach a level above what is considered acceptable.
One can understand the seriousness of the problem when we consider that the average level of exposure to smoke in the workplace is 270 times this acceptable risk level. The study concludes, in very cautious and conservative language, that habitual exposure to the smoke from one or more cigarettes per 60 employees per day would expose employees to risks of developing lung cancer from involuntary smoking greater than risks currently considered acceptable by American regulatory agencies for involuntary exposure to carcinogens in air, water or food.
That is the cautious and scientific way of saying that many people are being hurt. These include people under our jurisdiction; every federal employee of a Crown corporation or a company regulated by federal law. All of our employees at the House of Commons and the Senate are exposed to risks that would not be tolerated with other substances. The Government has suppressed this study. When I have raised the question, I
Adjournment Debate
have been told that either no legislation is necessary-that it will all be worked out in some type of friendly fashion-or that I should just be patient. I will not be patient with this level of damage that is being caused.
The other question is with respect to the costs. If the Government is not concerned about the health of Canadians, and it has shown precious little concern thus far, it should be concerned about the deficit. It should be concerned about the amount of money which is spent every year as a result of cigarette smoking. We know that $3 billion in taxes comes in every year from tobacco. However, the pay-outs are more than $8 billion a year to cover the costs of medicare, absences from work and so forth. In other words, every time a smoker pays $2.50 for a package of cigarettes, other people are paying $3.50 for the damage which is being done.
My concern is with the very specific costs incurred in the federal workplace. It is interesting to see that millions of dollars could be saved every year. The staff side of the National Joint Council has proposed to restrict smoking to smoking areas only with separate ventilation. One estimate has been done as a result of this proposal which assumes that there would be costs in doing these renovations. Such renovations would take five years to pay off. After these costs are paid off, the excess of annual benefits over cost would be $33 per employee. This comes to a total of $6 million a year for Government alone. If we add federal Crown corporations to this, it is another $12 million a year. If we look at the federal private sector, there is another $9 million a year to consider. Of course, if no smoking were permitted in the workplace at all, the savings would be enormous. One estimate in this respect amounts to over $2,000 per employee per year. There are others which are lower at $305 per employee per year and around $550 per employee per year. In other words, there are enormous costs involved. We are talking about hundreds of millions of dollars a year which could be saved by not permitting smoke in the workplace. These are just money savings. I am not even talking about the savings in terms of suffering and the harm which is caused to families of people who are hurt through tobacco-related diseases.
I call upon the Government to take this problem seriously and to bring in legislation to control smoke in the workplace. The level of 35,000 deaths per year from tobacco is unacceptable. A responsible Government would act promptly and vigorously to deal with this very serious problem. It is Canada's number one preventable health problem.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Gabrielle Bertrand (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: HEALTH-EXPOSURE OF WORKERS TO CIGARETTE SMOKE. (B) SMOKE-FREE OFFICES-ECONOMICS SAVINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like you to know that when tobacco was first introduced in Europe in the 16th century it was recommended for medicinal purposes. But it soon became apparent that the smoking habit was harmful because it was associated with health hazards.

March 18, 1986
Adjournment Debate
The fact that our diseases-lung cancer, myocardial infarct, peripheric vascular disease, and obstructive and chronic respiratory syndrome-have been directly linked to tobacco has caused deep concern among health specialists.
Tobacco smoke is a complex mixture in which more than
3,000	chemical substances have been identified. It is so complex that it is practically impossible to single out one specific substance as being the main factor with respect to any given disease caused by smoking. Still, a number of chemical substances known to be carcinogenic have indeed been detected in tobacco smoke.
In February 1985, the International Agency for Research on Cancer gathered a group of experts to assess the risk of cancer from smoking. In their judgment, there is enough evidence to say that smoke inhalation causes cancer in laboratory animals, and that it has been amply demonstrated that tobacco smoke is a carcinogenic agent in human beings.
With these findings in mind, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to point out that significant progress has been made in recent months to restrict smoking in the workplace. Employers realize that they can apply those restrictive measures at little or no cost, and that they stand to gain considerable benefits with respect to employee motivation and productivity in a saner and safer work environment.
The list of companies which apply a restraint policy is impressive and gets longer every day. Here are some of them: the Office of the Auditor General, the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, the Department of National Health and Welfare, the Insurance Corporation of British Columbia, Boeing of Canada Limited, Halifax Insurance, and Maritime Telephone and Telegraph.
In many cases, sections reserved for smokers are equipped with independent ventilation facilities.
In addition, some airlines have already banned smoking on all flights and VIA Rail has separate cars for non-smoking passengers.
The Department of National Health and Welfare has ongoing studies on the hazards of tobacco smoke. The Government will continue to rely on sound scientific data to draft its policies and plan its action concerning smoking and tobacco smoke.

subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF-TARIFF PLACED ON PRODUCT NOT PRODUCED IN CANADA
CUSTOMS TARIFF-TARIFF PLACED ON PRODUCT NOT PRODUCED IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, about a month ago, I raised a question in the House which essentially asked of the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) why it was that central Canadian steel suppliers and mills like Stelco and Algoma were allowed, because of their industrial practices, to smother new technology and companies using new technology on the West Coast. Actually, the issue is much older than some of us might suspect. It is probably as old as Confederation. For me the issue is at least nine years old.
In approximately 1977, because these companies suspected and only suspected that there would be a glut on the market of wide-flanged steel, they applied for and received from the Government an additional tariff of about 30 per cent which had the effect of almost destroying the fabricating industry in British Columbia. At that time, because of those additional tariffs on imported steel, it was possible for fabricating companies in Ontario to supply that kind of steel to a building company in Edmonton cheaper than it could be supplied from Vancouver. The companies in central Canada, because they had an unnecessary paranoia about pricing, almost destroyed the industry in British Columbia. New technology has now been added to the industry in B.C. and that has added a new wrinkle to the problem.
There is a company in my riding called Titan Steel and Wire. It has up-to-date, state-of-the-art technology for creating the kind of wire that is used in bridges and concrete works. The company cannot get raw materials from the Canadian steel mills as the Canadian product is inferior for its requirements. If you do not accept my word for that, Mr. Speaker, let me read telexes from the supplier in question. A telex dated November 21, 1985, from Stelco to Titan reads as follows:
Can meet all your requirements as specified except that we cannot guarantee tensile .. . our max coil weight is 1600 lbs-
Those are the two critical factors in the manufacture of this wire. A telex of November 26, 1985, from the same company to Titan reads as follows:
As far as coil size is concerned Stelco's is admittedly below that of new rod mills. As you know the rod mill was in the forefront of technology when it was installed. Newer mills around the world use the Stelmor process and gain competitive advantage from the production of larger and larger coils. However I doubt there is a rod mill in North America that could both produce the steel grade you require and process 4000 pound coils. Bethlehem might come the closest.
There is not one mill in North America that can do it, yet these companies refuse to allow the Department to change a tariff item so that Titan Steel and Wire can get the product from offshore and remain competitive.
It is a fact that the eastern mills are not interested in supplying this product. There is not even a salesman out on the West Coast who is trying to sell products from the East. Second, the eastern mills cannot supply the product, as these telexes have pointed out. Third, these mills are expecting new production lines to produce inferior products to suit the supplier rather than the new technology. I find that offensive to the market system. Since when does the open market system allow the supplier to dictate to the user what kind of products he can use? How in the world can Canada be on the cutting edge of new product lines if the supplier can dictate to the user?
March 18, 1986

According to the notes from the mill itself, the benefits of foreign suppliers are as follows: A 4,000-pound wire bod bundle is more efficient to use and results in a better quality finished product because there are less welds in a length of finished product; aluminum killed wire rod provides a better grain structure in the steel which results in a better quality finished product; and the chromium addition in the wire rod reduces tensile variation in the steel and improves the inner structure of the steel. When it comes to quality, why should the user not dictate what should be the quality rather than the supplier?
I guess what 1 find most offensive is that the officers in charge in the Department go to the supply companies in question for direction because government Departments do not have the technological expertise to determine whether or not there should be a change in tariffs. They go to Stelco and they go to Algoma for a definition. 1 find that offensive. If it is not conflict of interest, why do the heads of the tariffs division go to the user for a definition rather than to the supplier? Why do they go to Stelco? Why do they not go to Titan Steel and ask what the definition ought to be?
If we do not do this, we will surely move into a period of industrial stagnation. If the supplier can dictate to the user, we will never come to the cutting edge of technology. I have been on this issue, as I said, for about nine years; I am not about to quit now. I am looking to the day when the Department will recognize that the regions of the country have special needs which either the tariffs or the mills recognize.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CUSTOMS TARIFF-TARIFF PLACED ON PRODUCT NOT PRODUCED IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make regarding the questions raised by the Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen). The Minister of State (Finance) (Mrs. McDougall) who is responsible for tariff policy, as my colleague is aware, has examined the application made by the manufacturer of wire products in the Hon. Member's riding.
As my hon. friend pointed out, the company, Titan Steel & Wire Co. Ltd. in Surrey, has asked for a reduction in customs duty on the wire stock it imports to manufacture metal products such as strand screens, for use in pre-stressed concrete, and gravel screens. The Minister realizes that Titan wants to reduce its costs, and it would like to be able to help the company by granting it a tariff reduction.
Mr. Speaker, I shall now provide some general information that is very relevant to this particular case. Titan's request was considered in the light of legislation allowing the Governor-inCouncil to reduce or remove customs duty on items imported for use as manufacturing stock in Canada. The legislation is
Adjournment Debate
aimed at reducing the cost of the materials Canadian manufacturers need, in the event they cannot obtain such materials from Canadian producers, and if they can prove they need a tariff reduction to increase their competitive position. However, Mr. Speaker, tariff reductions of this kind are not granted when other Canadian companies might suffer adverse effects.
Regarding the tariff change requested by the company in my hon. friend's riding, when the Department of Finance asked the opinion of the parties concerned, as is usually done in such cases, two Canadian wire producers objected to the request being approved. They informed the Department that they produced wire stock that was directly competing with the kind of wire imported by Titan. Moreover, both companies felt that since they were also manufacturing metal products using the wire stock they produced, it would not be fair to remove customs duty on imported stock.
According to these two companies, this would give Titan a competitive edge which would be unfair, as you will understand, Mr. Speaker. On the other hand, they have offered to provide Titan with the type of wire it needs, and Titan has indicated its willingness to discuss the matter with them.
In view of these two points, the Minister of State for Finance has decided to reserve her decision following the request of the Hon. Member to give the parties involved enough time to examine the possibility that an agreement may be reached with Titan, which could then obtain the milled wire it needs from these Canadian producers.
The Hon. Member has indicated that Titan manufactures metal products mostly for export. In this regard, 1 must point out that, under certain provisions of Canadian law, companies can obtain a rebate or refund or fees paid on all material imported to produce goods for export. Titan can therefore obtain a refund of the duties paid on imported milled wire it uses in the manufacture of metal products for export. It seems to me that such a rebate does in fact reduce tarif costs as requested by Titan.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I hope that you will recognize that the position taken by the Minister as concerns the request made by the company through my colleague aims at solving a difficult problem and finding a solution which will be fair and equitable for all parties involved.
